t.6.14.1: Three nights passed for that Rāma as he lay on the ground strewn with kuśa grass, unwavering in his self-discipline.
t.6.14.2: Yet the sluggish Ocean did not then show himself to Rāma, though he had been duly worshipped by the devout and self-restrained Rāma.
t.6.14.3: Then Rāma, enraged at the ocean, the corners of his eyes turned red, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks, who stood near him.
t.6.14.4: Just look, Lakṣmaṇa, at the arrogance of this ignoble ocean, which, though it is being worshipped, does not show itself.
t.6.14.5: Tranquility, forbearance, uprightness and kindness of speech: these virtues of the good bear only the fruit of seeming weakness when shown toward those devoid of virtue.
t.6.14.6: The world honors the man who praises himself, who is wicked and insolent, who rushes about in every direction, and who wields the rod of punishment everywhere.
t.6.14.7: Neither renown nor glory can be won by conciliation in this world, O Lakṣmaṇa, nor can victory at the forefront of battle.
t.6.14.8: Today, O Saumitri, behold the ocean, the abode of makaras, its waters choked on every side by makaras pierced through by my arrows and floating about.
t.6.14.9: Look here, Lakṣmaṇa, at the huge bodies of the fishes, the trunks of the elephants, and the coils of the serpents, shattered by me.
t.6.14.10: Today, with my arrows, in a mighty battle, I shall dry up the ocean together with its masses of conches and pearl-oysters, together with its fish and makaras.
t.6.14.11: Because I am endowed with forbearance, this abode of sea-monsters takes me to be powerless. Shame on forbearance toward such a being!
t.6.14.12: Bring my bow, O Saumitri, and the arrows that are like venomous serpents! Today, enraged, I shall agitate the ocean, even though it cannot be agitated.
t.6.14.13: This abode of Varuṇa, whose bounds are set at its shores and which heaves violently with waves, I shall make boundless with my arrows.
t.6.14.14: Having spoken thus, Rāma, bow in hand, his eyes wide with anger, became unassailable, blazing like the fire at the end of an age.
t.6.14.15: Pressing hard upon his terrible bow and making the world tremble with his arrows, he released fierce shafts, as Śatakratu hurls his thunderbolts.
t.6.14.16: Those excellent arrows, of great velocity and blazing with splendor, enter the waters of the ocean, whose serpents are struck with terror.
t.6.14.18: Suddenly the great ocean became spread with garlands of mighty waves and crowded with conches and oyster shells, its billows rolling and churning amid smoke.
t.6.14.17: Then there arose a mighty and most terrible surge of the ocean, teeming with crocodiles and makaras, and accompanied by the roar of the wind.
t.6.14.20: Then the waves of the king of rivers, the ocean, teeming with crocodiles and makaras and resembling the Vindhya and Mandara mountains, rose up in their thousands.
t.6.14.19: The serpents, with blazing mouths and blazing eyes, were distressed, and so too were the Dānavas of great might who dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
t.6.14.21: The ocean became a turmoil: its masses of waves whirled about, its serpents and rākṣasas were thrown into panic, and its great crocodiles were heaved up from the depths.
